title: A Rocket Crashed Into the Moon — and NASA Just Found the Hole!
summary: Have you ever wondered what happens when a rocket hits the Moon? Well, now we know! On August 5, a piece of a SpaceX rocket slammed into the Moon's surface. It was the upper stage of a Falcon 9 rocket that had launched back in January 2025. The crash made a brand-new crater. But NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) couldn't just zoom over and take a picture right away. The orbiter circles the Moon from pole to pole once every two hours. The Moon slowly rotates underneath it. So LRO had to wait six whole days for the crater to spin into the right spot for a photo. And timing was super tricky! If the camera snapped just 10 seconds too early or too late, the crater would be about 10 miles away from the center of the picture. That's like trying to take a photo of a penny from a speeding car! When scientists finally got the images, they measured the crater. It's about 60 feet wide—that's as long as two school buses parked end to end. And it's less than 10 feet deep. The crash also threw up bright and dark streaks of dust and rocks. The dark stuff had been weathered by solar wind and tiny space rocks for a long time. The bright stuff came from deeper underground, where it was fresher. Finding the crater was a team effort. Astronomers around the world helped figure out where the rocket would hit. NASA's Planetary Defense team tested their prediction skills. They shared the location with South Korea's Danuri spacecraft, which took its own photo. NASA's prediction was off by only 0.6 miles—that's super close! Now scientists can study the crater to learn more about the Moon's surface. Who knew a rocket crash could be so exciting?
why_it_matters: Studying fresh craters helps scientists learn about the Moon, which could help future astronauts and missions that your generation might take part in.
